findings.description: The scoped-reverification feature (new in this diff, extensively documented as an intentional cost-saving change) has an undocumented failure mode: it assumes every finding's `locations` field resolves to at least one real repository file, and when that assumption fails the finding is not flagged as a corner case — it is silently and permanently treated as un-suspectable, which is a stronger exemption than 'not yet re-verified' and was not called out anywhere the design or tests describe the feature.
findings.after: pass_scope decides who stays open to re-check: `for f in findings_of(dir); id = f["id"]; (id in prev_open || f["lane"] == "scans") && continue; any(x -> x in touched, finding_files(root, f)) && push!(suspects, id); end`, and `finding_files` only returns a location string when `eachmatch(r"[A-Za-z0-9_][A-Za-z0-9_./\-]*\.[A-Za-z0-9]+", ...)` finds a substring that is ALSO `isfile(joinpath(root, f))`. When a finding's `locations` never yield such a string — a policy/architecture finding that cites a rule id, a section heading, or 'every consumer' rather than a bare `path:line` — `finding_files` returns `[]`, so `any(x -> x in touched, [])` is `false` for every future fix range: the id can never become a 'suspect' again, and `grade()`'s `carried = Dict(... for (i,e) in ... if !(String(i) in scope))` copies its old, once-only-verified entry forward for every subsequent pass without ever asking a verifier to look at it again. The same emptiness also exempts it from the new refusal gate: `unswept` does `isempty(named) && continue`, so a location-less open finding never blocks `pass open` even if nothing about it was ever touched.
findings.before: Base `pass_open`/`grade` both did `findings = findings_of(dir)` unconditionally — every pass re-verified every banked finding, closed or not, with no notion of a finding being exempt from re-verification.
findings.why_it_matters: The design intent stated in the same commit (ARCHITECTURE §6.2 step 7, PROTOCOL.md) is 'a closed finding can only regress where its own evidence lives, and the diff says whether anything went near it' — but that safety property silently degrades to 'never re-verified once closed' for exactly the findings whose evidence is not a bare file:line, which architecture/structure/policy findings routinely are. A round can close 'clean' while a finding closed in pass 1 is carried unexamined through every later pass, even though later fix passes may have touched the very files or logic the finding was about, just not under a location string the regex could resolve.
findings.title: A closed finding whose locations never resolve to a real file is exempt from re-verification forever, and from the new sweep-refusal too
findings.evidence: "(id in prev_open || f[\"lane\"] == \"scans\") && continue\n        any(x -> x in touched, finding_files(root, f)) && push!(suspects, id)" and "named = finding_files(root, f)\n        isempty(named) && continue" (src/CLI/Passes.jl)

findings.description: The fix correctly targets a real defect (the old check verified an unrelated fixed path instead of what `docs_build` actually runs), but its regex-based extraction of `.jl` tokens is narrower than the paths the package's own conventions require it to handle, so it swaps one false-pass defect for a new false-fail one on exactly the input shape (space-containing, quoted paths) this codebase calls out as a live concern.
findings.after: `scripts = [String(m.match) for m in eachmatch(r"[^\s\"']+\.jl", cfg["package"]["docs_build"])]` followed by `isfile(joinpath(root, s)) || push!(errs, "package.docs_build: $(repr(s)) does not exist")` for each match. The character class excludes both whitespace and quote characters, so a legitimately quoted path containing a space — e.g. `julia --project="docs" "docs/build script.jl"` — is not recovered as one token: the regex yields `"script.jl"` (confirmed by direct simulation of the same pattern), which is then checked at the wrong location and reported as not existing.

A consumer whose `docs_build` legitimately needs a quoted path with a space — the exact case the package's own rules anticipate — passed `check_paths`/`CFG.SURFACES` trivially under the old, command-independent check (since their seeded docs/make.jl existed) and now fails it with a spurious 'does not exist' error, blocking `gbg doctor`, `preflight`, and every round verb that gates on it, for a docs_build value that never changed.

findings.description: A new suite-level guard was added to catch a bare Markdown code span inside a Workflow prompt template. It is a real class and the guard catches it, but its stated contract (ordinary JavaScript is never a finding) is falsified by re-running it on the commonest JS form that ends a word before a template literal. Anchoring on the escape state rather than on the preceding character class, or excluding a `return`/`:` predecessor, would keep the true positives.

        @test iseven(count(==('`'), code))
findings.why_it_matters: The test's own comment says the check 'polices every future edit to eleven frozen scripts' and its second testset asserts 'valid JavaScript is not a finding'. All five negative probes happen to put the template literal after `=`, `(` or `,`. I ran the regex on the JavaScript forms it does not probe: `return \`ok\``, `if (x) return \`y\`` and `const x = cond ? \`a\` : \`b\`` are all FLAGGED, because `return` and `:` end in a character the lookbehind `[a-z,.;:] ` accepts. None of the 11 current scripts happens to contain one, so the suite is green today; the first author who writes `return \`…\`` in a Workflow script gets a red Pkg.test() with a message about Markdown code spans. In the other direction the class is also under-covered: a real bare span holding a comma, `)`, `}` or `$` — `\`read \`x, y\`\`` — is missed.

findings.evidence: Measured over all 11 workflow scripts: no hits (as the test asserts). findings.description: The guard removed is the config-driven whitelist itself. At base the scan asked exactly one question — is this `\mathbf{…}` string in the list this package declared? — and the tool held no literal of its own. At head the tool injects `\mathbf{1}` into every consumer's allowed set before the test, so no package can refuse it. If a fleet-wide standing exception is genuinely intended, it belongs where the other non-configurable facts live (ARCHITECTURE §5.5's non-configurable set, or the schema's `const`/`minItems` so an author who empties the list is told), not as a silent `push!` that leaves the key looking configurable. Note also the direction of the invariant the package states for itself: "A consumer holds data; the tool holds behaviour... No package string... in a Workflow script, a catalogue file or a policy file" — a package-visible notation literal now lives in the tool's scan body. The narrower point stands regardless of that reading: input that was previously refused (a `\mathbf{1}` under a config that did not admit it) now yields a clean scan.

findings.why_it_matters: SCAN.MATHBF is a `hard` scan: a hit is exit 1 from `gbg scan docs` and an `error()` from the `makedocs` wrapper. findings.description: The cost argument for scoping is real and is recorded (ARCHITECTURE §6.2 step 7: "the rc.1 round verified 56 findings ten times over where 90 verifications were owed"). What is not justified is the fail-open shape of the two predicates that implement it. Both `unswept` and `pass_scope` treat "I could not resolve a file for this finding" as "nothing to check", when the safe reading of an unresolvable location is the opposite: verify it. A minimal repair is to keep an id in scope whenever `finding_files` comes back empty, and to compute `touched` over the whole tree (or at least to include a named path that no longer exists as touched) rather than over `covered_paths`. Note the quantifier trap the brief names: none of this shows up as "input that used to work now behaves differently" — the affected findings are ones the previous pass CLOSED, so no other lane's question reaches them.

findings.description: The exemption itself is warranted — `git show <base>:policy/docs-rubric.md` shows the element-type clause already in RULE.DOC.ARGS_FORM at base, so this is not a rule invented to fit the code. The implementation is wider than the rule in the direction that fails silently: it exempts on a name pattern instead of on the presence of the prose binding the rule requires. Gating `eltype_kw` on `prosed` (i.e. exempt only when the docstring actually binds the arguments in running prose) would restore the rule's meaning and cost nothing. The same edit is also narrower than the rule in the loud direction, which is worth stating because it is the same line: for a two-argument docstring with a `T` keyword written in bullets — clean at base, since `wants_bullets` was true — head now takes the `!wants_bullets && bulleted` branch and hits with "bind them in running prose, not bullets", converting the rule's permission into an obligation.

findings.why_it_matters: Take `f(x; T = Float64)` with a docstring that documents nothing about its arguments — no `The arguments are:` bullets and no `The arguments are \`…\`` prose. With `ARGS_THRESHOLD = 3`: base computed `wants_bullets = (2 >= 3) || !isempty(["T"]) = true`, `bulleted = false`, and pushed the hard hit "`f` takes 1 positional and 1 keyword argument(s): the bulleted `The arguments are:` form, not prose". Head computes `eltype_kw = true`, so `wants_bullets = (2 >= 3) || (true && !(true && 2 < 3)) = false`; `bulleted` and `prosed` are both false, no branch fires, and the docstring is clean. RULE.DOC.ARGS_FORM's exemption is "a single element-type keyword bound in one prose clause" — a permission granted to a docstring that HAS the prose clause. The scan checks neither that the prose clause exists nor that the keyword is an element type; it matches a name against `^(T|eltype|.*_type)$`, which also admits keywords like `arg_type`, `hit_type` or `round_type` that carry no element semantics at all. The rule's own gate (any keyword forces the argument to be documented somehow) is therefore removed for a class the scan cannot identify.

findings.description: The stated motive ("a package function always wins its own name") is reasonable and the docstring names three examples in this very package, but the change is to a public harness engine that this repository does not exercise: there is no `test/method_parity.jl` and no `method_parity_baseline.toml` under `test/`, and the tool's declared deviations put the allocation and traffic contracts out of scope here. Its only consumers are the four science packages, whose frozen baselines were not and could not be regenerated in this change set. That leaves a computed count altered with no oracle anywhere in the tree, and the first evidence either way will be a consumer's `Pkg.test()` after the next `gbg bump`. Confidence is medium, not high, because the practical reach depends on whether `isdefined(pkg, name)` already resolved a Base-exported name at the umbrella — in which case the reorder is inert for exported generics and bites only for the shadowed submodule case described above.

When a package extends a Base generic (`show`, `size`, `length`, `read`) AND also has a same-named binding of its own inside one of its submodules, the resolved `f` changes from the Base generic — whose method table contains the package's added methods — to the package's own function, whose table does not. locations: fixture/GBG Fixture/src/FixtureC.jl:41-49 (new `span` function and its docstring)
findings.description: The diff adds a new `span(options)` fixture function whose docstring, after the ordinary identity/argument/returns prose, appends an explanatory paragraph about why the SCAN.ARGS_FORM parenthesis-matching bug in GBGCodingTools' own scanner used to mis-parse this exact signature. That explanation is meta-commentary for a future maintainer reading the source, not documentation of what `span` does — but it lives inside the rendered docstring body, so it is exactly as reachable to a REPL reader as the rest of the text, in a package whose own rubric (RULE.DOC.NO_DEAD_REFS, RULE.DOC.SELF_CONTAINED, RULE.DOC.HOME_ORDER's exclusion list) exists specifically to keep this kind of content out.
findings.after:
"""
    span(options) -> (lo, hi)

The iteration bounds of an [`Options`](@ref) record; internal, so it needs no page home. The argument
`options` is the record. Returns the pair.

Two arguments and a returned tuple: RULE.DOC.ARGS_FORM binds fewer than three in running prose, and
SCAN.ARGS_FORM must read the parameter list as the parenthesis that closes the first one — a parser
that stopped at the last `)` counted the return tuple as three more parameters and demanded bullets.
"""
span(options::Options) = (1, options.iterations)
findings.before: (no such function or docstring existed at base; FixtureC.jl had no `span` binding)
findings.why_it_matters: A reader who runs `?span` (or opens this docstring on any page it is ever homed to) hits two bare identifiers — `RULE.DOC.ARGS_FORM` and `SCAN.ARGS_FORM` — that resolve to nothing outside `policy/RULES.toml` and `catalog/scans.toml`; the paragraph is also architectural rationale about a bug in the SCANNER's own parenthesis-matching, which RULE.DOC.HOME_ORDER's own exclusion list ("implementation internals ... architectural rationale") explicitly keeps out of a function docstring. This is the one instance of this pattern anywhere in the fixture — every other fixture docstring reads as clean, self-contained prose — so it is a new precedent, not a continuation of an existing one, and it evades the existing SCAN.DEAD_REF pattern (which only matches `§`, `docs/`, `ALLCAPS.md`, `inspiration/`) even though it is exactly the class of thing RULE.DOC.NO_DEAD_REFS and RULE.DOC.SELF_CONTAINED are written to prevent.
